outcome: Nothing in the window settles or moves this statement as worded: the large-graph case was proved by Csaba, Kühn, Lo, Osthus and Treglown (arXiv January 2014, Memoirs of the AMS 2016), before the window, and every in-window event I found concerns a neighbouring question (the overfull conjecture, Kotzig's perfect 1-factorisation, multigraph versions) rather than this bullet.
problem_asks: (i) For each odd n: every k-regular simple graph on 2n vertices, for every k with n ≤ k ≤ 2n−1, is 1-factorable (its edge set splits into k pairwise disjoint perfect matchings, equivalently its chromatic index is k). (ii) For each even n: every k-regular simple graph on 2n vertices, for every k with n−1 ≤ k ≤ 2n−1, is 1-factorable. The two parts are both required. The statement quantifies over all n with no lower bound on n, so it is not restricted to sufficiently large n. It asserts the conjecture for every such k, not only a bound on k.

events.what_happened: Chetwynd and Hilton, 'Regular graphs of high degree are 1-factorizable', Proc. London Math. Soc. (2), pp. 193–206 (1985). Abstract fragments on the Lancaster record (opened): the conjecture is well known for degree 2n−1 or 2n−2 (graphs of order 2n); the paper shows it for degree 2n−3, 2n−4 and 2n−5, and states a further result (degree condition garbled in the record and not readable by me). Wikipedia's Graph factorization article (opened) attributes to this paper the statement that k ≥ 12n/7 implies 1-factorability (2n vertices). I did not read the paper itself. The usual attribution of the question is to Dirac in the 1950s, which the paper reports second-hand.
events.delivers: Restricted to the top of the degree range: for regular graphs on 2n vertices, degrees 2n−3, 2n−4 and 2n−5 (per the abstract fragments). Wikipedia cites a further sub-range k ≥ 12n/7 (about 0.857 times the vertex count), which I did not verify in the paper.
events.remains: Every other degree in the bullet's range, in particular k from n up to about 6n/7 (and the parts between), and every n.
events.time_since_posted: 41 years at 11 October 2026; I found no public re-examination of this paper.
events.direction: Proves the conjecture in the restricted high-degree range it covers; cuts in favour of the conjecture; no counterexample involved.

sources.title: Lancaster eprint record: Chetwynd & Hilton, Regular graphs of high degree are 1-factorizable (1985)
Graph factorization (Wikipedia)

events.what_happened: Chetwynd and Hilton, '1-factorizing regular graphs of high degree: an improved bound', Discrete Math. 75 (1989) 103–112, as cited on Mohar's problem page (opened). Per that page, it proves the conjecture under the stronger assumption that k is at least c·n/2 with c = √7 − 1 (about 1.646), where n is the order of the graph, so k ≥ ((√7−1)/2)·V(G) ≈ 0.823·V(G). The page also says Hilton later reported smaller constants, citing a private communication. I did not read the 1989 paper.
events.delivers: Degrees k ≥ ((√7−1)/2)·V, with V the vertex count, per the Mohar statement (the page gives no size restriction). This is a sub-range above V/2, not the whole bullet range.
events.remains: Degrees between V/2 and about 0.823·V, and the bullet's other cases.
events.direction: Proves the conjecture in a high-degree sub-range; cuts in favour of the conjecture.

sources.title: Mohar, One Factorization and Hamiltonian Factorization Conjecture (problem page, revised 2002)

events.what_happened: Perković and Reed, 'Edge coloring regular graphs of high degree', Discrete Math. 165–166 (1997) 567–578 (DOI 10.1016/S0012-365X(96)00202-6). Secondary sources (search snippets; the DOI redirected and I did not read the article) state: for every ε > 0 there is N(ε) such that every Δ-regular simple graph of even order n > N(ε) with Δ ≥ (1/2+ε)n is 1-factorable. One snippet credits this jointly with Häggkvist; I could not find a Häggkvist paper.
events.delivers: Asymptotic: for large even order, degrees at least (1/2+ε)·V. This is the bullet's threshold V/2 up to an additive εV, not the exact threshold.
events.remains: Degrees in [V/2, (1/2+ε)V) for large V, the exact threshold, and all small orders.
events.direction: Asymptotic support for the conjecture; cuts in favour of it on the large-order range.
people: Häggkvist (credited in one snippet; no paper found)

events.what_happened: E. R. Vaughan, 'An asymptotic version of the multigraph 1-factorization conjecture', arXiv:1010.5192, submitted 25 October 2010, one version (opened). Abstract (paraphrased by the fetch tool): for every multiplicity bound r and every ε > 0 there is N(r, ε) such that every regular multigraph of order 2n with multiplicity at most r and degree at least (1+ε)rn is 1-factorable for n ≥ N(r, ε). The abstract says this generalises results of Perković–Reed and of Plantholt–Tipnis.
events.delivers: Asymptotic 1-factorisation for regular multigraphs of bounded multiplicity r, for large n, at degree (1+ε)rn (order 2n). This is a different hypothesis (multiplicity r, not simple graphs). The abstract does not state the r = 1 case separately.
events.remains: The simple-graph statement as worded, the exact multigraph threshold rn, and all small n.
events.direction: Asymptotic support for a multigraph analogue; does not settle the simple-graph bullet as stated.

sources.title: Vaughan, An Asymptotic Version of the Multigraph 1-Factorization Conjecture

events.what_happened: Csaba, Kühn, Lo, Osthus and Treglown, 'Proof of the 1-factorization and Hamilton decomposition conjectures', arXiv:1401.4159 (parts II–IV: 1401.4164, 1401.4178, 1401.4183). The arXiv record (opened) gives v1 submitted 16 January 2014 and v2 revised 22 October 2014; the v2 comment says the four parts are combined into one publication to appear in the Memoirs of the AMS. Part III's v1 (1401.4178) is also dated 16 January 2014 in a search snippet. The 1-factorization theorem as summarised by the arXiv record and by the Birmingham record: for all sufficiently large even n, every D-regular graph G on n vertices with D ≥ 2⌈n/4⌉ − 1 has a 1-factorization (equivalently χ′(G) = D). The sources say the bound is best possible and that the conjecture was explicitly stated by Chetwynd and Hilton. Published: Memoirs of the American Mathematical Society, vol. 244, no. 1154 (2016), 164 pages, DOI 10.1090/memo/1154, e-pub 21 June 2016 (Birmingham record, opened; the AMS page refused automated fetch). Translated to this bullet's notation (graph on N = 2n vertices), the threshold 2⌈N/4⌉ − 1 equals n when n is odd and n − 1 when n is even, which are exactly the bullet's thresholds, for all sufficiently large n.
events.revisions: arXiv 1401.4159 v1 16 Jan 2014 (77 KB); v2 22 Oct 2014 (231 KB, current; combines the four parts); part III 1401.4178 v1 16 Jan 2014 (search snippet). Memoirs AMS vol. 244 no. 1154, published June 2016.
events.delivers: The 1-factorization statement for all sufficiently large graphs on an even number of vertices, at the bullet's exact degree thresholds (with the ceiling reading, see doubts). Covers every n ≥ n0 for a universal constant n0; I did not find n0 made explicit in the sources I read. The same paper also proves the Hamilton decomposition conjecture and an optimal Hamilton-cycle packing result, which are not this bullet.
events.remains: Every n below the (unquantified) size threshold n0, which is the part of the bullet's 'for all n' that the proof does not reach. I found no small-order result covering all such n (see the Kaski–Östergård event for one finite instance).

events.doubts: No active doubt found: no erratum, no public objection, no withdrawal, no gap identified by anyone in the sources I read. Signals for the judging pass: (a) I read only the arXiv summary and the Birmingham record, not the Memoir or the full arXiv text, so the exact theorem statement and n0 are not verified against the paper; (b) sources differ on floor versus ceiling in the threshold. One search snippet gives 2⌊N/4⌋ − 1, which is false: two disjoint copies of K_(2t+1) are 2t-regular on 4t+2 vertices and have no perfect matching, so the ceiling reading is the consistent one; (c) a Kühn-hosted revision PDF (web.mat.bham.ac.uk/D.Kuehn/1factrevision.pdf) exists but its text was not extractable to me; its extracted headings contain unresolved '??' cross-references, so I cannot say what it revises.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for all sufficiently large graphs on an even number of vertices, at the bullet's degree thresholds (ceiling reading). Cuts in favour of the conjecture. No counterexample involved. Sharpness: the sources say the bound is best possible, and the two-cliques example shows the degree bound cannot be lowered.

events.what_happened: Shan, 'Towards the Overfull Conjecture', arXiv:2308.16808, v1 submitted 31 August 2023, v2 1 Sep 2023, v3 20 Sep 2023, v4 5 Sep 2024 (opened). The version history is as the fetch returned it. v4 proves the Overfull Conjecture (Chetwynd–Hilton 1986: a graph with Δ > |V|/3 has chromatic index Δ iff it has no overfull subgraph) for graphs on n ≥ n0 vertices with Δ ≥ (1−ε)n, 0 < ε ≤ 1/14, with no minimum-degree condition. The abstract says it implies Vizing's average-degree conjecture for that class. Comments field: arXiv admin note on text overlap with arXiv:2205.08564 and arXiv:2105.05286.
events.revisions: v2 1 Sep 2023; v3 20 Sep 2023; v4 5 Sep 2024 (the in-window version). I did not compare v1–v3 with v4; I cannot say whether the minimum-degree condition was present earlier.
events.delivers: The Overfull Conjecture for large graphs with Δ ≥ (1−ε)V, for all graphs in that class (not only regular). Sources I read (Wikipedia Graph factorization, opened) say the overfull conjecture implies the 1-factorization conjecture. So this is a route to the bullet in the range k ≥ (1−ε)V, not a direct proof of the bullet.
events.remains: The overfull conjecture for Δ between V/3 and (1−ε)V, and the 1-factorization statement itself, which this paper does not state.

disputes.summary: The question is attributed to Dirac in the 1950s (Mohar's page; Chetwynd and Hilton report it as already discussed by Dirac) and first stated explicitly by Chetwynd and Hilton (1985). I did not find a primary source for Dirac's statement.

Threshold conventions differ across sources. Wikipedia (2n vertices): k ≥ n for n odd, k ≥ n−1 for n even. Mohar (order n): k ≥ n/2. CKLOT (order N): D ≥ 2⌈N/4⌉ − 1, which equals the Wikipedia thresholds with N = 2n. One search snippet gives 2⌊N/4⌋ − 1, which is false (two disjoint copies of K_(2t+1) are 2t-regular on 4t+2 vertices with no perfect matching).

Chetwynd–Hilton partial thresholds are reported inconsistently: Wikipedia gives k ≥ 12n/7 for 2n vertices (1985); Mohar gives k ≥ ((√7−1)/2)·V for the 1989 paper; a search snippet attributes the (√7−1)/2 result variously to 1985 and 1989. I did not resolve this from the original papers.

Wikipedia nests Kotzig's perfect 1-factorization conjecture under this bullet. Several search snippets and the 2026 Cheng–Sgueglia preprint treat the two as different. I record Kotzig events as neighbouring questions.

summary:
The statement is the Chetwynd–Hilton / Dirac 1-factorization conjecture in Wikipedia's form: a k-regular graph on 2n vertices, with k ≥ n for n odd or k ≥ n−1 for n even, is 1-factorable. Its substantive history is before the window. Partial results: Chetwynd and Hilton 1985 (degrees 2n−3 to 2n−5, plus a garbled further condition; Wikipedia credits k ≥ 12n/7) and 1989 (k ≥ ((√7−1)/2)·V ≈ 0.823V, per Mohar's page); Perković and Reed 1997 (asymptotic, degree ≥ (1/2+ε)V for large order, from snippets only). Csaba, Kühn, Lo, Osthus and Treglown (arXiv 16 January 2014; v2 22 October 2014; Memoirs AMS vol. 244 no. 1154, 2016) prove it for all sufficiently large graphs on an even number of vertices with degree threshold 2⌈N/4⌉ − 1, which is exactly the bullet's threshold in this notation. One snippet gives the floor version 2⌊N/4⌋ − 1; that version is false, so I take the ceiling reading as the correct one. Later sources treat the result as settled: Wikipedia's Graph factorization article (last edited 19 March 2026) says CKLOT confirmed it for sufficiently large n, and the July 2026 Chen–McDonald–Shan preprint (arXiv 2607.02270) cites it as verified for all sufficiently large graphs. I found no erratum, no Lean formalisation, no public objection, and no withdrawal. The Wikipedia list (read in full) still shows the bullet, with the statement's wording, in its unsolved section, with no citation.

Close call: CKLOT covers only sufficiently large n, and the bullet quantifies over all n. I found no explicit size bound n0 in the sources I read, and no small-order result beyond Kaski and Östergård's 2005 classification of order-12 one-factorizations for r ≤ 6 and r ∈ {10, 11} (the abstract does not list r = 7, 8, 9).

In-window events are all neighbouring questions, not this bullet. The closest is the Chen–McDonald–Shan overfull-conjecture result (2 July 2026), which covers large graphs with Δ ≥ (1+ε)|V|/2, a range CKLOT already covers. Kotzig's perfect 1-factorisation (Glock–Sgueglia 2 October 2025; Cheng–Sgueglia 10 July 2026) is Wikipedia's child bullet, not this one.

AI: no source for this bullet names an AI system, so none_found is true. That rests on the search results and the abstract-level sources I read; the CKLOT full text was not read. The neighbouring AI item is Jing's multigraph edge-colouring preprint (arXiv 2308.15588, versions from 2026), whose abstract says two theorems were verified by an AI-assisted audit using 'OpenAI's GPT-6 Pro model in ChatGPT'. That is verification of a human-written proof, not load-bearing mathematics, and it concerns a different question, so ai.systems is empty for that event. Other 2026 AI results surfaced by search (Knuth's note on Claude Opus 4.6 and a directed Hamiltonian-cycle decomposition; a GPT-5.6 claim on the cycle double cover conjecture) concern other problems and were seen only in secondary snippets. The Gemini case-study paper (arXiv 2602.03837) has a perfect-matching section on regular bipartite graphs that I did not read. Dirac's 1950s attribution has no primary source I could find.
competing_reading: The bullet is resolved. Its thresholds are exactly CKLOT's (ceiling reading), the literature and the Wikipedia Graph factorization article treat it as proved, and the only gap is a finite set of small graphs that the bullet does not name. The opposite reading: the bullet asks for every n with no size bound, the proof gives only sufficiently large n with an unquantified n0, and the Wikipedia unsolved list still marks it open, so as written it is not established. A third reading: the in-window overfull-conjecture work (Chen–McDonald–Shan, 2026) adds to the large-graph picture, but only in a range CKLOT already covers, so it changes nothing for the all-n statement.
what_would_settle_it: The Memoir text: whether the theorem gives an explicit n0 and the ceiling threshold exactly. Any survey, or the authors, stating the status of the all-n statement. The AMS page (refused automated fetch) for any erratum. The Kühn revision PDF (unreadable to me here). Any complete small-order verification below n0, if it exists. The full text of Chen–McDonald–Shan's 2026 introduction and of Jing's 2026 version, to confirm the citation and the AI sentence verbatim.

judgement.why: The statement quantifies over all n, so CKLOT (2014, Memoirs AMS 2016, journal of record → digested) settles a restriction (all sufficiently large n at the exact thresholds): case, not whole, and before the snapshot. Chetwynd–Hilton 1985/1989 and Perković–Reed 1997 are journal-published restrictions to degree sub-ranges or large order: case. Multigraph, pseudorandom, counting, Hamilton-decomposition, overfull-conjecture and Kotzig results answer changed questions: variant. Chen–McDonald–Shan 2026 is the closest post-snapshot event, but it proves the overfull conjecture, not this statement, in a range CKLOT already covers, so it is variant too. Kaski–Östergård is a finite check (instances). Jing's GPT audit only verified the proof, so it is none, and the event is a variant anyway. No post-snapshot event touches the statement itself.
judgement.doubts: Whether the residual small-n gap is substantive is debatable. If small cases had been exhausted, CKLOT would be whole and digested, giving open_stale rather than open. The record finds no explicit n0 and no small-order completion, so I answered case. Perković–Reed is known only from snippets.
